analysis.one_liner: Gives adults a refundable $3,000 yearly tax credit, paid monthly, for low and middle incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2019 with 13 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021 — no hearing, no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a refundable tax credit of $3,000 per year for adults, with the amount shrinking as income rises: a single person keeps the full $3,000 up to $30,000 of income and loses it entirely by $50,000, while married couples get double those figures. Taxpayers can choose to receive the credit as monthly payments during the year instead of a lump sum at tax time, and the payments would not count as income or assets when applying for other federal benefits. The bill also sets up a $30 million-a-year grant program so volunteer groups can prepare tax returns free of charge for low-income filers. As a statement of intent, it says the cost should be covered by repealing most of the 2017 Republican tax law (keeping only the parts that help people earning under $100,000) and by a fee on banks with more than $50 billion in assets.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with low and middle incomes: singles earning up to $50,000 and married couples up to $100,000 would get cash back, up to $3,000 (or $6,000 for a couple) per year, delivered monthly if they choose. Low-income taxpayers who struggle with tax preparation would also benefit from expanded free volunteer help. People receiving public assistance would benefit because the credit payments cannot be counted against their eligibility for those programs.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable credit of $3,000 per eligible adult, phased out for a single filer between $30,000 and $50,000 of adjusted gross income, with joint filers receiving double those amounts and all figures rising with inflation [S2, S3]
Requires the IRS to set up a program of monthly advance payments, so families can receive the money throughout the year rather than once at tax time [S2, S3]

Bars the credit from being counted as income or resources for eligibility for federal, state, or locally funded assistance programs, so receiving it cannot cost a household its other benefits [S2, S3]

Creates a Community Volunteer Income Tax Assistance Matching Grant Program of up to $30 million per fiscal year for free, IRS-certified tax preparation for low-income and underserved taxpayers [S2, S3]

States the House's position that the cost should be fully offset by repealing the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act except for provisions benefiting people with incomes under $100,000, and by a fee on financial institutions with more than $50 billion in assets [S2, S3]

analysis.who_pays: Under the bill's stated pay-fors, the cost would fall on corporations and higher-income households that benefited from the 2017 tax law (whose provisions would be repealed except for those helping people earning under $100,000) and on the largest banks, which would pay a fee. However, the bill contains no actual revenue provisions — the pay-fors are only a non-binding statement of the House's sense — so the fiscal cost would depend on later legislation.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, corporations, and large banks

drawbacks.text: The offsets are non-binding: the pay-fors appear only as a 'sense of the House of Representatives' statement, and the bill text contains no revenue provisions, so the estimated cost would not actually be paid for by this bill alone [S3]
The pay-fors would repeal most of the 2017 tax cuts, raising taxes on corporations and on households earning above $100,000, including many upper-middle-income families [S2, S3]

Monthly advance payments create a repayment risk: because the credit is calculated on the prior year's income, a household whose income rises during the year could receive more than it is owed and have to pay the difference back at tax time — the same reconciliation problem that complicated the ACA's advance premium tax credits (general mechanism; the advance-payment and reconciliation rules are in the bill [S3])
The phaseout begins at $30,000 of income for singles, so the credit's full benefit is confined to lower-income adults and fades before reaching middle-income workers earning $50,000 to $100,000 [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is substantial and targeted: up to $3,000 per adult in cash for tens of millions of low and middle-income households, delivered monthly if they choose, with protection for other public benefits. The honest weaknesses are design ones: the bill does not actually pay for itself (the offsets are only a statement of intent), and advance payments could force some households whose incomes rose to return part of the money later. The stated pay-fors — repealing the 2017 corporate and upper-income tax cuts and a fee on the largest banks — would be a real and significant tax increase on those groups if enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or moved it to the floor before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on June 27, 2019, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors including Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pramila Jayapal, and Ayanna Pressley [S3, S4, S5]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax credits [S1, S5]
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S5]
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died with it [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, the 2017 tax law's cuts for corporations and higher-income households remained in place and the largest banks avoided any fee. Low and middle-income adults received no new credit, and free tax-preparation grants were never funded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations, high earners, and large banks

for.name: Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing the $3,000 refundable middle-class tax credit with monthly advances and free tax-prep grants

for.name: 13 of 231 House Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors (Cicilline, Cohen, Dingell, Garcia, Hastings, Jackson Lee, Jayapal, Lee, Norton, Ocasio-Cortez, Pressley, Pocan)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no cosponsor from the other party

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation; chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 27, 2019 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it died there when the Congress ended [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; since the bill never got a vote, no roll-call split exists, but support ran entirely along one party's progressive wing.

industries.industry: Corporations and higher-income households benefiting from the 2017 tax cuts
industries.note: The bill's stated pay-for would repeal the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act except for provisions helping people earning under $100,000, reversing the corporate rate cut and upper-income tax cuts. This is where the bill's funding was meant to come from.

industries.industry: Large financial institutions (over $50 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill proposes a Treasury-set fee on any bank with more than $50 billion in consolidated assets as part of its stated offsets. The largest banks bear the fee; smaller banks are untouched.

industries.industry: Paid tax preparation industry serving low-income filers
industries.note: A $30 million-a-year grant program would expand free volunteer tax preparation for low-income and underserved taxpayers, competing with paid preparers and refund-advance products that charge those same customers. The industry's interest in this provision runs against taxpayers getting free help.
